question: A 72-year-old man with progressive exertional chest tightness and brief fainting spells has a harsh systolic murmur that peaks mid-systole and radiates to his neck. On exam his carotid upstroke is delayed and diminished. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the symptoms and signs of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Degenerative narrowing of the left ventricular outflow valve
options.rationale: Aortic outflow obstruction from degenerative valve disease produces a harsh crescendo–decrescendo systolic murmur radiating to the neck with delayed, diminished carotid upstroke (pulsus parvus et tardus) and causes angina and syncope as described.

options.text: Ischemic papillary muscle rupture causing sudden valve incompetence
options.rationale: Papillary muscle rupture causes acute regurgitation with pulmonary edema and hypotension rather than a delayed carotid upstroke and a crescendo–decrescendo systolic murmur; it would be correct only if acute severe regurgitant signs were present.

options.text: Myxomatous prolapse of the mitral valve with late systolic click
options.rationale: Mitral leaflet prolapse produces a mid‑systolic click and possible late systolic murmur radiating to the axilla, not a harsh systolic murmur radiating to the neck with delayed carotid upstroke; it would be correct only if a click and axillary radiation were described.

options.text: Rheumatic fusion of mitral leaflets causing low‑pitched diastolic rumble
options.rationale: Mitral stenosis causes an opening snap and low‑pitched diastolic rumble at the apex with left lateral decubitus positioning, not a harsh systolic murmur radiating to the neck; it would be correct only if diastolic apex findings were present.

options.text: Tricuspid annular dilation producing holosystolic murmur at left sternal border
options.rationale: Tricuspid regurgitation yields a holosystolic murmur best heard at the left sternal border with signs of right‑sided failure, not a crescendo–decrescendo systolic murmur radiating to the carotids; it would be correct only with right‑sided failure signs.

question: A 58-year-old woman with a history of long-standing hypertension reports increasing shortness of breath on exertion and chest discomfort. On exam she has a laterally displaced, sustained apical impulse and a harsh systolic murmur best heard at the upper right sternal border. Which pathophysiologic change best explains her left ventricular findings?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the diagnostic approach to mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease including the appropriate diagnostic tests.

options.text: Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy from chronic outflow obstruction
options.rationale: Chronic obstruction of the aortic outflow increases afterload, producing concentric LV hypertrophy to maintain stroke volume; echocardiography is the diagnostic test of choice for valve assessment.

options.text: Eccentric left ventricular dilation from chronic volume overload
options.rationale: Eccentric dilation occurs with chronic regurgitant lesions (volume overload) rather than fixed outflow obstruction; this would be correct if a regurgitant murmur and widened pulse pressure were described.

options.text: Right ventricular hypertrophy from pulmonary valve obstruction
options.rationale: RV hypertrophy follows right‑sided outflow obstruction and would present with right‑sided findings, not a sustained apical impulse and a murmur at the upper right sternal border; it would be correct only with right‑sided signs.

options.text: Left atrial enlargement from impaired mitral inflow
options.rationale: LA enlargement is characteristic of mitral stenosis with diastolic rumble and opening snap, not a harsh systolic murmur and sustained apical impulse; it would be correct only with mitral stenosis features.

options.text: Acute myocardial wall rupture causing localized bulge
options.rationale: Acute wall rupture causes catastrophic hemodynamic collapse and would not produce a chronic sustained apical impulse; it would be correct only in the setting of recent transmural infarction and shock.

question: A 45-year-old woman with a history of connective tissue disease has a bounding peripheral pulse and a wide difference between systolic and diastolic pressures. Which auscultatory finding is most consistent with her condition?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the symptoms and signs of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: High‑pitched blowing diastolic murmur at the left lower sternal border
options.rationale: Aortic valve insufficiency produces a high‑pitched, blowing, decrescendo diastolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border and is associated with widened pulse pressure and bounding pulses.

options.text: Low‑pitched rumbling diastolic murmur at the apex
options.rationale: A low‑pitched diastolic rumble at the apex indicates mitral stenosis with an opening snap, not the widened pulse pressure and bounding pulses seen in aortic regurgitation; it would be correct only with mitral stenosis signs.

options.text: Harsh crescendo–decrescendo systolic murmur at upper right sternal border
options.rationale: A harsh systolic murmur at the upper right sternal border suggests aortic stenosis, which causes a diminished delayed carotid upstroke rather than bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure; it would be correct only with AS features.

options.text: High‑pitched holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border
options.rationale: A holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border suggests tricuspid regurgitation, which is associated with right‑sided failure signs rather than bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure; it would be correct only with TR findings.

options.text: Mid‑systolic click followed by late systolic murmur at the apex
options.rationale: A mid‑systolic click with late systolic murmur indicates mitral valve prolapse and is not associated with widened pulse pressure and bounding peripheral pulses; it would be correct only if MVP symptoms were present.

question: A patient with chronic aortic valve leakage is being followed. Which echocardiographic or measurement threshold from the lecture indicates high risk and suggests referral for surgical correction before irreversible dysfunction?
cited_learning_objective: Outline a treatment plan for mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Left ventricular end systolic diameter greater than 50 millimeters
options.rationale: The lecture states that an LV end‑systolic diameter > 50 mm or EF   70 mm is a high‑risk threshold mentioned for mitral regurgitation, not for aortic regurgitation; it would be correct only if the question asked about mitral regurgitation.

options.text: Aortic valve area less than 0.7 square centimeters
options.rationale: A valve area of 0.7 cm² is cited as critical for aortic stenosis severity, not the surgical threshold for chronic aortic regurgitation; it would be correct only for severe aortic stenosis assessment.

options.text: Pulmonary artery systolic pressure above 50 millimeters mercury
options.rationale: Pulmonary pressures are relevant for pulmonary or secondary tricuspid disease but are not the specific high‑risk LV size or EF thresholds used to time surgery for aortic regurgitation; it would be correct only with pulmonary hypertension context.

options.text: Left atrial diameter exceeding 60 millimeters
options.rationale: Left atrial enlargement is important in mitral disease and atrial fibrillation risk but is not the lecture's stated high‑risk criterion for timing surgery in aortic regurgitation; it would be correct only if mitral disease thresholds were requested.

question: A 30-year-old woman with a family history of connective tissue disorder has palpitations and intermittent chest pain. Cardiac auscultation reveals a mid‑systolic click with a late systolic murmur. Which management approach is most appropriate for a patient with mild findings and no significant regurgitation?
cited_learning_objective: Outline a treatment plan for mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Conservative observation without intervention and periodic echocardiography
options.rationale: Most patients with mild mitral valve prolapse require no treatment; the lecture recommends observation and echocardiographic monitoring, with endocarditis prophylaxis only if significant regurgitation is present.

options.text: Immediate surgical valve replacement with prosthetic ring
options.rationale: Surgical repair or replacement is reserved for significant regurgitation or declining LV function; immediate surgery would be appropriate only if severe MR or LV dysfunction were documented.

options.text: Lifelong anticoagulation with warfarin
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is indicated for atrial fibrillation or mechanical prosthetic valves, not for uncomplicated mitral valve prolapse without AF; it would be correct only if the patient had AF or a mechanical valve.

options.text: Aggressive afterload reduction with vasodilators immediately
options.rationale: Afterload reduction is used in significant regurgitant lesions to reduce forward flow burden, but is not indicated for asymptomatic mild MVP without MR; it would be correct only with documented significant MR.

options.text: Endocarditis prophylaxis for all future dental procedures
options.rationale: The lecture advises prophylaxis only when MR is present; universal prophylaxis for all MVP patients is not recommended and would be correct only if significant MR were present.

question: A 65-year-old man with severe calcific left outflow obstruction is scheduled for valve intervention. Which preoperative test is emphasized in the lecture as commonly performed to evaluate concomitant coronary disease?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the diagnostic approach to mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease including the appropriate diagnostic tests.

options.text: Cardiac catheterization to assess coronary artery disease
options.rationale: The lecture notes that patients with aortic stenosis often undergo cardiac catheterization to determine if significant coronary artery disease is present prior to valve replacement.

options.text: Pulmonary function testing for lung parenchymal disease
options.rationale: Pulmonary function tests assess lung disease but are not the routine preoperative test emphasized for assessing coronary disease in aortic stenosis; it would be correct only if pulmonary comorbidity were the primary concern.

options.text: Transcranial Doppler to evaluate cerebral embolic risk
options.rationale: Transcranial Doppler is not a standard preoperative test for coronary assessment before valve surgery; it would be correct only if evaluating specific embolic phenomena.

options.text: Right heart catheterization to measure pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
options.rationale: Right heart cath measures pulmonary pressures and is used in pulmonary hypertension assessment, not routinely to evaluate coronary artery disease prior to aortic valve replacement; it would be correct only with suspected pulmonary vascular disease.

options.text: Carotid duplex ultrasound to screen for carotid stenosis
options.rationale: Carotid duplex screens for carotid disease but is not the primary test to assess coronary anatomy before valve replacement; it would be correct only if carotid disease were suspected.

question: A patient with chronic severe mitral valve narrowing develops hemoptysis and progressive exertional dyspnea. Which auscultatory feature described in the lecture is most characteristic of this condition?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the symptoms and signs of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: High‑pitched opening snap followed by low‑pitched diastolic rumble at the apex
options.rationale: Mitral stenosis classically produces a high‑pitched opening snap and a low‑pitched rumbling diastolic murmur best heard at the apex with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position.

options.text: Harsh systolic crescendo–decrescendo murmur at the upper right sternal border
options.rationale: That murmur is typical of aortic stenosis, not mitral stenosis; it would be correct only if outflow obstruction signs were present.

options.text: High‑pitched blowing diastolic murmur at the left lower sternal border
options.rationale: A high‑pitched diastolic murmur at the left lower sternal border indicates aortic regurgitation, not mitral stenosis; it would be correct only with AR features.

options.text: Mid‑systolic click with late systolic murmur radiating to axilla
options.rationale: A mid‑systolic click and late systolic murmur are seen in mitral valve prolapse, not in mitral stenosis; it would be correct only with MVP findings.

options.text: Holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the left axilla
options.rationale: A holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla indicates mitral regurgitation, not mitral stenosis; it would be correct only if MR were the dominant lesion.

question: A 50-year-old patient with chronic severe mitral regurgitation is asymptomatic but echocardiography shows progressive left ventricular dilation. According to the lecture, which echocardiographic measurement would most strongly prompt consideration of surgical repair?
cited_learning_objective: Outline a treatment plan for mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Left ventricular end diastolic diameter greater than 70 millimeters
options.rationale: The lecture lists LV end‑diastolic diameter > 70 mm as a high‑risk criterion in mitral regurgitation that suggests the need for surgical repair to prevent irreversible LV dysfunction.

options.text: Left ventricular end systolic diameter greater than 50 millimeters
options.rationale: An LV end‑systolic diameter > 50 mm is cited for aortic regurgitation risk, not the specific mitral regurgitation threshold; it would be correct only for AR context.

options.text: Ejection fraction above 65 percent
options.rationale: A high EF is not an indication for surgery; surgery is prompted by declining EF or excessive chamber dilation, so this would be correct only if EF were reduced below the lecture's threshold.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation with normal left atrial size
options.rationale: AF increases risk and may prompt anticoagulation, but AF with normal LA size alone is not the lecture's surgical threshold for MR; it would be correct only if LV size or function were also abnormal.

options.text: Pulmonary artery systolic pressure mildly elevated
options.rationale: Mild pulmonary hypertension alone is not the primary surgical trigger for MR per the lecture; it would be correct only if severe pulmonary hypertension or LV dysfunction were present.

question: A 60-year-old man presents with sudden onset severe shortness of breath and hypotension after chest trauma. Echocardiography shows abrupt severe leakage across the aortic valve. According to the lecture, what is the most appropriate immediate management step?
cited_learning_objective: Outline a treatment plan for mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Urgent afterload reduction and emergent surgical valve replacement
options.rationale: Acute aortic regurgitation is a medical and surgical emergency; the lecture recommends vasodilators and diuretics for stabilization followed by emergent valve replacement because the LV cannot acutely compensate.

options.text: Conservative outpatient observation with serial echocardiography
options.rationale: Observation is inappropriate for acute severe AR with hemodynamic instability; it would be correct only for chronic, compensated AR without instability.

options.text: Immediate percutaneous balloon valvuloplasty
options.rationale: Balloon valvuloplasty is mainly used for congenital noncalcified stenosis in younger patients, not for acute severe AR from trauma; it would be correct only for suitable stenotic lesions.

options.text: Start long‑term vasodilator therapy and defer surgery indefinitely
options.rationale: While vasodilators help temporarily, definitive management of acute severe AR is urgent surgical replacement; deferring surgery indefinitely would be correct only if the patient were stable and surgery contraindicated.

options.text: Administer thrombolytics for presumed valve thrombosis
options.rationale: Thrombolysis is not indicated for traumatic acute AR; it would be correct only if prosthetic valve thrombosis were documented as the cause.

question: A 40-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic fever presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and palpitations. ECG shows atrial fibrillation. Which valvular lesion from the lecture most commonly leads to atrial fibrillation and why?
cited_learning_objective: List the etiologies of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Mitral valve narrowing causing left atrial enlargement and pressure overload
options.rationale: Mitral stenosis increases left atrial pressure and size, predisposing to atrial fibrillation; the lecture notes rheumatic disease as the most common cause of mitral stenosis.

options.text: Aortic valve narrowing causing concentric left ventricular hypertrophy
options.rationale: Aortic stenosis causes LV hypertrophy and symptoms like angina and syncope but does not primarily cause left atrial enlargement and AF; it would be correct only if mitral inflow were impaired.

options.text: Tricuspid regurgitation causing right atrial enlargement and systemic congestion
options.rationale: Tricuspid regurgitation leads to right atrial enlargement and right‑sided symptoms rather than left atrial enlargement and AF; it would be correct only with right‑sided arrhythmias.

options.text: Pulmonic valve stenosis causing right ventricular pressure overload
options.rationale: Pulmonic stenosis affects the right heart and is not a common cause of left atrial enlargement or AF; it would be correct only with right‑sided atrial arrhythmias.

options.text: Mitral valve prolapse causing isolated ventricular arrhythmias
options.rationale: MVP can cause palpitations and autonomic symptoms but is not the classic cause of AF from LA enlargement; it would be correct only if significant MR and LA enlargement were present.

question: A 55-year-old patient with chronic aortic stenosis is noted to be preload dependent. Which clinical action described in the lecture could precipitate hemodynamic deterioration in these patients?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the diagnostic approach to mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease including the appropriate diagnostic tests.

options.text: Aggressive diuresis causing intravascular volume depletion
options.rationale: The lecture emphasizes that aortic stenosis patients are preload dependent and can decompensate with dehydration or aggressive diuretics, which reduce LV filling and cardiac output.

options.text: Initiation of beta‑blocker therapy for rate control
options.rationale: Beta‑blockers may be used cautiously but are not specifically highlighted as precipitating collapse in AS; they would be problematic only if they caused severe bradycardia or hypotension.

options.text: Starting long‑term ACE inhibitor therapy for afterload reduction
options.rationale: Afterload reduction is more relevant to regurgitant lesions; ACE inhibitors are not singled out as causing acute deterioration in AS unless profound hypotension occurs.

options.text: Performing a Valsalva maneuver during physical exam
options.rationale: Valsalva transiently reduces venous return and can alter murmurs but is not typically a cause of sustained hemodynamic collapse in AS; it would be correct only if the patient were already unstable.

options.text: Administering intravenous fluids rapidly to increase preload
options.rationale: Rapid IV fluids would usually support preload and improve hemodynamics in preload‑dependent AS, not precipitate deterioration; it would be correct only if fluid overload caused pulmonary edema.

question: A 28-year-old intravenous drug user presents with fever and new holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border with signs of right‑sided volume overload. Which valve and likely etiology from the lecture best fit this presentation?
cited_learning_objective: List the etiologies of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Tricuspid valve regurgitation due to infective endocarditis
options.rationale: The lecture notes endocarditis as a cause of tricuspid regurgitation; IV drug use predisposes to right‑sided infective endocarditis producing a holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border and signs of RV failure.

options.text: Mitral valve prolapse from myxomatous degeneration
options.rationale: MVP causes a mid‑systolic click and possible MR radiating to the axilla, not the left sternal border holosystolic murmur with right‑sided failure; it would be correct only with classic MVP findings.

options.text: Aortic regurgitation from bicuspid valve endocarditis
options.rationale: Aortic regurgitation produces a diastolic blowing murmur and wide pulse pressure rather than a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border; it would be correct only if diastolic findings were present.

options.text: Pulmonic stenosis from congenital leaflet fusion
options.rationale: Pulmonic stenosis causes systolic outflow obstruction and right‑sided pressure signs but typically presents earlier in life and with a systolic ejection murmur, not a holosystolic murmur from regurgitation; it would be correct only with congenital history.

options.text: Functional tricuspid regurgitation from left‑sided heart failure
options.rationale: Functional TR from left‑sided failure causes right‑sided signs but is less likely in an IV drug user with fever and new murmur; it would be correct only if there were chronic left‑sided disease causing RV dilation.

question: A 70-year-old patient with severe aortic stenosis is asymptomatic but echocardiography shows a valve area of 0.6 cm². According to the lecture, how should this valve area be classified?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the diagnostic approach to mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease including the appropriate diagnostic tests.

options.text: Critical aortic outflow obstruction
options.rationale: The lecture defines critical (severe) aortic stenosis as a valve area around 0.7 cm²; a measured area of 0.6 cm² falls into the critical/severe category.

options.text: Mild aortic valve narrowing
options.rationale: Mild aortic narrowing would have a much larger valve area; this option would be correct only with a valve area near normal values.

options.text: Normal aortic valve area
options.rationale: Normal aortic valve area is approximately 3 cm²; 0.6 cm² is far below normal and would be correct only if measurement units were misreported.

options.text: Moderate aortic valve stenosis
options.rationale: Moderate stenosis corresponds to intermediate valve areas larger than the critical threshold; this would be correct only if the area were closer to 1.0–1.5 cm².

options.text: Functional aortic regurgitation
options.rationale: Aortic regurgitation is characterized by diastolic murmur and widened pulse pressure, not a reduced valve area; it would be correct only if regurgitant flow rather than stenosis were documented.

question: A patient with chronic aortic regurgitation develops exertional chest pain. Which mechanism described in the lecture best explains angina in this setting despite patent coronary arteries?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the symptoms and signs of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Increased left ventricular wall stress and oxygen demand from volume overload
options.rationale: Chronic aortic regurgitation causes LV dilation and hypertrophy, increasing wall stress and myocardial oxygen demand which can produce angina even with normal coronaries, as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Coronary embolization from valvular vegetations
options.rationale: Coronary emboli can cause angina but are not the typical mechanism in chronic AR; this would be correct only if endocarditis with embolization were documented.

options.text: Reduced coronary perfusion due to low systemic blood pressure
options.rationale: While hypotension can reduce coronary perfusion, chronic AR usually features widened pulse pressure and not persistent hypotension; this would be correct only with sustained low perfusion pressures.

options.text: Left atrial ischemia from mitral inflow obstruction
options.rationale: LA ischemia is not a recognized cause of exertional angina in AR; it would be correct only if mitral inflow obstruction and LA ischemia were present.

options.text: Right ventricular ischemia from pulmonary hypertension
options.rationale: RV ischemia from pulmonary hypertension causes right‑sided symptoms, not the exertional chest pain typical of LV demand ischemia in AR; it would be correct only with severe pulmonary vascular disease.

question: A 35-year-old woman with suspected rheumatic heart disease presents with fever and migratory polyarthritis two weeks after a sore throat. Which set of clinical features from the lecture comprises the Jones criteria for acute rheumatic fever?
cited_learning_objective: List the etiologies of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Carditis, arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules
options.rationale: The lecture lists the Jones criteria as carditis, arthritis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules for acute rheumatic fever following group A strep infection.

options.text: Pericarditis, pulmonary embolism, hemoptysis, clubbing, cyanosis
options.rationale: These findings are not the Jones criteria; pericarditis can occur in pancarditis but the listed combination is incorrect and would be correct only with different diagnostic criteria.

options.text: Endocarditis, renal failure, petechiae, splinter hemorrhages, fever
options.rationale: While endocarditis and fever may be present, renal failure and petechiae are not part of the Jones major criteria; this would be correct only in a different infectious context.

options.text: Mitral stenosis, aortic stenosis, tricuspid stenosis, pulmonic stenosis, heart block
options.rationale: These are valvular lesions rather than the Jones criteria for acute rheumatic fever; it would be correct only if listing chronic valvular sequelae.

options.text: Arthralgia, fever, leukocytosis, elevated ESR, positive throat culture
options.rationale: These are minor or supportive findings rather than the major Jones criteria; they would be correct only as part of minor criteria or supportive evidence.

question: A patient with chronic severe mitral regurgitation develops pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular failure. According to the lecture, which sequence best describes the hemodynamic progression leading to right‑sided failure?
cited_learning_objective: Review of Basic Concepts

options.text: Left atrial volume overload → pulmonary venous congestion → pulmonary hypertension → right ventricular failure
options.rationale: Mitral regurgitation causes LA dilation and increased pulmonary venous pressure, leading to pulmonary hypertension and subsequent RV failure, as outlined in the lecture.

options.text: Right atrial dilation → systemic venous congestion → pulmonary edema → left ventricular failure
options.rationale: This sequence reverses the sidedness and is inconsistent with MR pathophysiology; it would be correct only with primary right‑sided valvular disease causing systemic congestion first.

options.text: Aortic outflow obstruction → LV dilation → pulmonary venous congestion → RV failure
options.rationale: Aortic stenosis primarily affects the LV and does not directly cause pulmonary venous congestion unless secondary mitral disease occurs; it would be correct only with concomitant mitral involvement.

options.text: Pulmonary embolism → acute RV failure → left atrial enlargement → mitral stenosis
options.rationale: Pulmonary embolism causes acute RV strain but does not lead to mitral stenosis; this would be correct only in a contrived sequence not described in the lecture.

options.text: Left ventricular systolic failure → decreased forward flow → systemic hypotension → tricuspid regurgitation
options.rationale: While LV failure can lead to secondary right‑sided issues, this sequence does not reflect the classic progression from MR to pulmonary hypertension and RV failure described in the lecture; it would be correct only with primary LV systolic failure.

question: A 68-year-old woman with severe aortic stenosis is being counseled about valve replacement options. According to the lecture, which statement about prosthetic valves is accurate regarding long‑term management?
cited_learning_objective: Outline a treatment plan for mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Mechanical valves require lifelong anticoagulation with a target INR of 2.5 to 3.5
options.rationale: The lecture states mechanical prosthetic valves are durable but require anticoagulation, with a goal INR of 2.5–3.5 to reduce thrombosis risk.

options.text: Tissue valves always require lifelong warfarin anticoagulation
options.rationale: Tissue (bioprosthetic) valves generally do not require lifelong anticoagulation; this would be correct only if the patient had another indication for anticoagulation such as AF.

options.text: Mechanical valves are less durable than tissue valves
options.rationale: Mechanical valves are more durable than tissue valves; this option would be correct only if the durability relationship were reversed.

options.text: All prosthetic valves eliminate the need for echocardiographic surveillance
options.rationale: Echocardiography is the best way to monitor prosthetic valve function and is still required; this would be correct only if valves were infallible, which they are not.

options.text: Antiplatelet therapy is contraindicated after tissue valve implantation
options.rationale: Aspirin is often recommended for tissue valves per the lecture; contraindication would be correct only with specific bleeding risks.

question: A 62-year-old man with chronic aortic regurgitation has a bounding pulse and head bobbing with each heartbeat. Which eponymous sign from the lecture corresponds to the head bobbing phenomenon?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the symptoms and signs of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Musset sign
options.rationale: Musset sign is the head bobbing with each pulse described in aortic regurgitation and is listed among peripheral signs in the lecture.

options.text: Corrigan pulse
options.rationale: Corrigan (water‑hammer) pulse refers to a bounding pulse with rapid upstroke and collapse, not specifically head bobbing; it would be correct only if describing the pulse quality.

options.text: Quincke pulse
options.rationale: Quincke pulse denotes capillary nailbed pulsations in AR, not head bobbing; it would be correct only if nailbed pulsations were observed.

options.text: Duroziez sign
options.rationale: Duroziez sign is a to‑and‑fro femoral murmur in AR, not head bobbing; it would be correct only with femoral auscultatory findings.

options.text: Muller sign
options.rationale: Muller sign is uvular pulsation during systole in AR, not head bobbing; it would be correct only if uvular pulsation were noted.

question: A 48-year-old man with suspected infective endocarditis has a new diastolic murmur and signs of heart failure. The lecture lists several causes of acute aortic regurgitation. Which of the following is NOT listed as a cause of acute aortic valve insufficiency in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: List the etiologies of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy
options.rationale: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy is not listed in the lecture as a cause of acute aortic regurgitation; the lecture lists endocarditis, trauma, aortic dissection, and prosthetic valve dysfunction as acute causes.

options.text: Infective endocarditis
options.rationale: Infective endocarditis is explicitly listed as a cause of acute aortic regurgitation in the lecture; it would be wrong only if endocarditis were absent.

options.text: Aortic dissection
options.rationale: Aortic dissection is cited as a cause of acute AR in the lecture; it would be wrong only if dissection were excluded clinically.

options.text: Trauma to the aortic valve
options.rationale: Trauma is included among acute causes of AR in the lecture; it would be wrong only if trauma were not present.

options.text: Prosthetic valve dysfunction
options.rationale: Prosthetic valve dysfunction is listed as a cause of acute AR in the lecture; it would be wrong only if the patient had a native valve without prosthesis.

question: A 55-year-old woman with chronic mitral stenosis is found to have blood‑tinged sputum. Which mechanism from the lecture best explains hemoptysis in this condition?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the symptoms and signs of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Elevated pulmonary venous pressure causing pulmonary capillary rupture
options.rationale: Mitral stenosis raises left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures, leading to pulmonary congestion and possible pulmonary apoplexy or hemoptysis as described in the lecture.

options.text: Septic emboli from left‑sided endocarditis
options.rationale: Septic emboli can cause hemoptysis but are not the typical mechanism in chronic mitral stenosis; this would be correct only if endocarditis with embolization were documented.

options.text: Pulmonary embolism causing infarction
options.rationale: Pulmonary embolism can cause hemoptysis via infarction but is unrelated to the chronic LA pressure elevation in MS; it would be correct only with evidence of thromboembolism.

options.text: Bronchiectasis from recurrent infections
options.rationale: Bronchiectasis causes hemoptysis but is not the lecture's mechanism for hemoptysis in MS; it would be correct only with chronic pulmonary infection history.

options.text: Left ventricular failure causing systemic hypoperfusion
options.rationale: LV failure causes pulmonary edema but hemoptysis in MS is specifically linked to pulmonary venous hypertension and capillary rupture; this would be correct only with severe LV failure causing pulmonary hemorrhage.

question: A 70-year-old man with severe aortic stenosis is scheduled for valve replacement. The lecture notes that outcomes are best when which preoperative cardiac function is preserved?
cited_learning_objective: Outline a treatment plan for mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Left ventricular systolic function
options.rationale: The lecture states that valve replacement for aortic stenosis has the best outcomes when left ventricular function is preserved prior to surgery.

options.text: Right ventricular diastolic function
options.rationale: While RV function matters, the lecture specifically emphasizes preserved LV function as the key predictor of better outcomes for AS surgery; this would be correct only if RV function were the focus.

options.text: Left atrial contractile function
options.rationale: LA contractile function is not highlighted as the primary determinant of surgical outcome in AS; it would be correct only if mitral disease predominated.

options.text: Pulmonary vascular resistance
options.rationale: Pulmonary vascular resistance affects right‑sided disease outcomes but is not the lecture's stated main predictor for AS valve replacement success; it would be correct only with severe pulmonary hypertension.

options.text: Aortic root compliance
options.rationale: Aortic root properties influence AR but are not the lecture's emphasized preoperative predictor for AS replacement outcomes; it would be correct only if root pathology were the main issue.

question: A 45-year-old man with suspected mitral stenosis undergoes echocardiography showing a valve area of 0.9 cm². According to the lecture, how should this valve area be categorized?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the diagnostic approach to mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease including the appropriate diagnostic tests.

options.text: Critical mitral valve narrowing
options.rationale: The lecture defines critical mitral stenosis as a valve area < 1 cm²; an area of 0.9 cm² meets the criterion for critical/severe MS.

options.text: Mild mitral valve narrowing
options.rationale: Mild MS would have a larger valve area; this would be correct only with a valve area closer to normal.

options.text: Normal mitral valve area
options.rationale: Normal mitral valve area is approximately 4–6 cm²; 0.9 cm² is far below normal and would be correct only if units were misreported.

options.text: Moderate mitral valve narrowing
options.rationale: Moderate stenosis corresponds to valve areas larger than the critical threshold; this would be correct only if the area were nearer to 1.5 cm².

options.text: Functional mitral regurgitation
options.rationale: Mitral regurgitation is a volume lesion with holosystolic murmur, not defined by a reduced valve area; it would be correct only if regurgitant flow were documented.

question: A patient with chronic aortic regurgitation is treated medically to reduce afterload. Which class of medications mentioned in the lecture is appropriate to decrease afterload in this setting?
cited_learning_objective: Outline a treatment plan for mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Vasodilators such as ACE inhibitors or hydralazine
options.rationale: The lecture recommends vasodilators (ACE inhibitors, hydralazine) to decrease afterload in patients with aortic regurgitation to reduce regurgitant volume and LV workload.

options.text: Loop diuretics as sole long‑term therapy
options.rationale: Diuretics relieve congestion but do not primarily reduce afterload; they would be correct only as adjunctive therapy for symptomatic volume overload.

options.text: Beta‑blockers to increase contractility
options.rationale: Beta‑blockers reduce heart rate and may be used in some contexts but are not the lecture's primary afterload‑reducing agents for AR; this would be correct only if rate control were the main goal.

options.text: Calcium channel blockers to increase preload
options.rationale: Calcium channel blockers do not increase preload and are not specified as first‑line afterload reducers for AR in the lecture; it would be correct only with specific hemodynamic rationale.

options.text: Long‑acting nitrates to increase systemic vascular resistance
options.rationale: Nitrates decrease preload and afterload but are not the lecture's emphasized agents; stating they increase systemic resistance is incorrect and would be correct only if their hemodynamic effect were mischaracterized.

question: A 70-year-old patient with multiple valve disease from prior rheumatic fever is being evaluated. The lecture warns that multiple valve replacement is associated with which of the following outcomes?
cited_learning_objective: List the etiologies of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Higher operative mortality compared with single valve replacement
options.rationale: The lecture notes that multiple valve replacement is associated with higher mortality than single valve procedures, reflecting increased surgical risk.

options.text: Lower long‑term complication rates than single valve replacement
options.rationale: Multiple valve replacement carries greater complexity and risk, not lower complication rates; this would be correct only if outcomes paradoxically improved, which the lecture does not state.

options.text: No need for anticoagulation regardless of prosthesis type
options.rationale: Anticoagulation needs depend on prosthesis type (mechanical vs tissue) and are not eliminated by multiple replacements; it would be correct only if all valves were tissue and no other indications existed.

options.text: Guaranteed resolution of pulmonary hypertension
options.rationale: Valve replacement may improve hemodynamics but does not guarantee reversal of pulmonary hypertension; it would be correct only if pulmonary vascular changes were fully reversible.

options.text: Lower risk of endocarditis compared with native valves
options.rationale: Prosthetic valves carry risk of endocarditis; multiple replacements do not reduce this risk and would be correct only if prostheses were immune to infection.

question: A 66-year-old man with aortic stenosis is asked about less invasive surgical options. The lecture mentions a minimally invasive approach for valve replacement. Which statement best reflects the lecture's guidance about patient selection?
cited_learning_objective: Outline a treatment plan for mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Minimally invasive valve replacement is an option but advanced age increases morbidity
options.rationale: The lecture notes that minimally invasive approaches are available for valve replacement, but advanced age is associated with higher morbidity and must be considered in selection.

options.text: Minimally invasive replacement is contraindicated in all calcified valves
options.rationale: The lecture does not state an absolute contraindication for calcified valves; this would be correct only if specific anatomic constraints precluded the approach.

options.text: Minimally invasive replacement eliminates the need for postoperative monitoring
options.rationale: Postoperative monitoring remains necessary regardless of approach; this would be correct only if monitoring were truly unnecessary, which the lecture does not claim.

options.text: Minimally invasive replacement requires no preoperative coronary assessment
options.rationale: Coronary assessment is often performed regardless of surgical approach; omitting it would be correct only if the patient had no coronary risk factors and imaging excluded disease.

options.text: Minimally invasive replacement is preferred in all patients over open surgery
options.rationale: Preference depends on patient factors; the lecture does not endorse universal preference and this would be correct only if minimally invasive approaches were superior for all patients.

question: A 52-year-old woman with severe mitral stenosis is being considered for percutaneous balloon valvuloplasty. According to the lecture, which etiology most commonly underlies mitral stenosis and often makes patients candidates for this procedure?
cited_learning_objective: List the etiologies of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Rheumatic fever causing leaflet fusion and commissural fusion
options.rationale: The lecture states rheumatic fever is the most common cause of mitral stenosis, producing leaflet fusion, thickening, and commissural fusion amenable to balloon valvuloplasty in suitable patients.

options.text: Myxomatous degeneration causing floppy leaflets
options.rationale: Myxomatous degeneration causes mitral prolapse and regurgitation rather than stenosis; it would be correct only if prolapse were the lesion.

options.text: Carcinoid tumor causing isolated mitral stenosis
options.rationale: Carcinoid typically affects right‑sided valves and can cause tricuspid or pulmonic lesions, not classic rheumatic MS; it would be correct only with unusual left‑sided carcinoid involvement.

options.text: Congenital bicuspid mitral valve causing early stenosis
options.rationale: Congenital causes exist but are less common than rheumatic disease; this would be correct only if congenital anatomy were documented.

options.text: Annular calcification from aging causing isolated MS
options.rationale: Annular calcification more commonly contributes to mitral regurgitation or mixed disease rather than classic rheumatic MS; it would be correct only with imaging confirming calcific obstruction.

question: A 60-year-old patient with severe mitral regurgitation has an LV end‑systolic diameter of 48 mm and an EF of 52%. According to the lecture, which statement best reflects surgical timing considerations?
cited_learning_objective: Outline a treatment plan for mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Consider mitral valve repair before further LV dilation or EF decline
options.rationale: The lecture emphasizes that surgery is indicated when LV dimensions exceed high‑risk thresholds or EF declines; early repair is favored to prevent irreversible LV dysfunction.

options.text: Defer surgery until EF falls below 30 percent
options.rationale: Waiting for severe EF decline worsens prognosis; the lecture recommends intervention before significant LV dysfunction, so this would be correct only if surgical risk outweighed benefit.

options.text: Proceed only with valve replacement if heavy calcification is present
options.rationale: Repair with annuloplasty is preferred when feasible; replacement is chosen when repair is not possible (e.g., heavy calcification), so this would be correct only if repair were impossible.

options.text: Manage solely with afterload reduction indefinitely
options.rationale: Medical therapy can temporize but does not replace surgery when LV dilation or EF decline occurs; it would be correct only if the patient were not a surgical candidate.

options.text: Delay intervention until pulmonary hypertension develops
options.rationale: Pulmonary hypertension is a complication and not the preferred trigger for delaying surgery; intervention is ideally before irreversible changes like pulmonary vascular remodeling occur.

question: A 50-year-old patient with suspected tricuspid stenosis has prominent jugular venous distention, hepatomegaly, and peripheral edema. Which auscultatory finding from the lecture is most consistent with tricuspid stenosis?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the symptoms and signs of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Opening snap with a soft, high‑pitched diastolic murmur
options.rationale: Tricuspid stenosis produces an opening snap and a soft, high‑pitched diastolic murmur, though it may be obscured by louder left‑sided murmurs; right‑sided failure signs are typical.

options.text: Low‑pitched rumbling diastolic murmur at the apex
options.rationale: A low‑pitched diastolic rumble at the apex indicates mitral stenosis, not tricuspid stenosis; it would be correct only with left‑sided findings.

options.text: Harsh systolic murmur radiating to the neck
options.rationale: A harsh systolic murmur radiating to the neck is characteristic of aortic stenosis, not tricuspid stenosis; it would be correct only with AS features.

options.text: High‑pitched blowing diastolic murmur at left lower sternal border
options.rationale: A high‑pitched diastolic murmur at the left lower sternal border suggests aortic regurgitation, not tricuspid stenosis; it would be correct only with AR signs.

options.text: Holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla
options.rationale: A holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla indicates mitral regurgitation, not tricuspid stenosis; it would be correct only if MR were present.

question: A 67-year-old man with severe aortic stenosis is noted to have diminished carotid pulses and a delayed upstroke. Which physical exam descriptor from the lecture best matches this carotid finding?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the symptoms and signs of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Pulsus parvus et tardus
options.rationale: Pulsus parvus et tardus describes a diminished and delayed carotid upstroke seen in aortic stenosis and is specifically mentioned in the lecture.

options.text: Corrigan pulse
options.rationale: Corrigan pulse is a bounding water‑hammer pulse seen in aortic regurgitation, not the delayed weak pulse of AS; it would be correct only with AR features.

options.text: Quincke pulse
options.rationale: Quincke pulse refers to nailbed capillary pulsations in AR, not delayed carotid upstroke; it would be correct only if capillary pulsations were observed.

options.text: Kussmaul sign
options.rationale: Kussmaul sign is a paradoxical rise in JVP on inspiration seen in RV dysfunction, not the carotid pulse abnormality of AS; it would be correct only with RV failure.

options.text: Duroziez sign
options.rationale: Duroziez sign is a to‑and‑fro femoral murmur in AR, not the delayed carotid upstroke of AS; it would be correct only with femoral auscultatory findings.

question: A 58-year-old woman with chronic aortic regurgitation demonstrates a low‑pitched diastolic murmur at the apex in addition to the classic high‑pitched diastolic murmur. Which named murmur from the lecture explains this apical finding and its mechanism?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the symptoms and signs of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Austin Flint murmur from regurgitant jet impinging on mitral leaflet
options.rationale: The Austin Flint murmur is a low‑pitched diastolic murmur at the apex caused by the regurgitant aortic jet interfering with mitral valve opening, as described in the lecture.

options.text: Graham Steell murmur from pulmonary valve regurgitation
options.rationale: Graham Steell murmur is associated with pulmonary regurgitation and pulmonary hypertension, not the apical low‑pitched murmur of AR; it would be correct only with pulmonic findings.

options.text: Duroziez murmur from femoral artery to‑and‑fro flow
options.rationale: Duroziez sign is a femoral to‑and‑fro murmur in AR, not the apical Austin Flint murmur; it would be correct only with femoral auscultation findings.

options.text: Opening snap from mitral stenosis
options.rationale: An opening snap is a high‑pitched sound in mitral stenosis, not the low‑pitched apical murmur caused by AR; it would be correct only with MS features.

options.text: Mid‑systolic click from mitral valve prolapse
options.rationale: A mid‑systolic click is seen in MVP and is unrelated to the diastolic apical murmur of AR; it would be correct only with MVP findings.

question: A 45-year-old patient with suspected prosthetic valve dysfunction presents with hemolysis and new murmur. The lecture lists several complications of prosthetic valves. Which of the following is included among those complications?
cited_learning_objective: List the etiologies of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Thrombosis, stenosis or insufficiency, endocarditis, hemolysis
options.rationale: The lecture enumerates thrombosis, stenosis or insufficiency, endocarditis, and hemolysis as complications of prosthetic heart valves.

options.text: Pulmonary embolism, deep venous thrombosis, systemic vasculitis, myocarditis
options.rationale: These are not the specific prosthetic valve complications listed in the lecture; they would be correct only in different clinical contexts.

options.text: Primary pulmonary hypertension, bronchiectasis, pleural effusion, empyema
options.rationale: These pulmonary conditions are unrelated to the prosthetic valve complications emphasized in the lecture; they would be correct only with primary pulmonary disease.

options.text: Renal failure, hepatic failure, pancreatitis, adrenal insufficiency
options.rationale: These systemic organ failures are not the prosthetic valve complications listed; they would be correct only if multisystem disease were present.

options.text: Cerebral aneurysm, subarachnoid hemorrhage, carotid dissection, temporal arteritis
options.rationale: These cerebrovascular and vasculitic conditions are not prosthetic valve complications per the lecture; they would be correct only in unrelated neurologic disease.

question: A 70-year-old patient with chronic aortic regurgitation is noted to have Quincke pulse on exam. What physical sign does Quincke pulse describe as listed in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the symptoms and signs of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Capillary nailbed pulsations visible with each heartbeat
options.rationale: Quincke pulse refers to nailbed capillary pulsations seen in aortic regurgitation and is explicitly mentioned among peripheral signs in the lecture.

options.text: Head bobbing synchronous with the pulse
options.rationale: Head bobbing is Musset sign, not Quincke pulse; it would be correct only if describing Musset sign.

options.text: Uvula pulsation during systole
options.rationale: Uvula pulsation is Muller sign, not Quincke pulse; it would be correct only if uvular movement were observed.

options.text: Bounding carotid pulse with rapid collapse
options.rationale: A bounding water‑hammer pulse is Corrigan pulse, not Quincke pulse; it would be correct only if describing the carotid pulse quality.

options.text: To‑and‑fro femoral artery murmur
options.rationale: A to‑and‑fro femoral murmur is Duroziez sign, not Quincke pulse; it would be correct only with femoral auscultatory findings.

question: A 34-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has mitral valve leaflet thickening and regurgitation. The lecture lists several causes of mitral regurgitation. Which cause is identified as the most common?
cited_learning_objective: List the etiologies of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Myxomatous valve degeneration
options.rationale: The lecture states that myxomatous valve degeneration is the most common cause of mitral regurgitation.

options.text: Rheumatic fever
options.rationale: Rheumatic fever can cause MR but is not listed as the most common cause; it would be correct only if rheumatic disease predominated in the population.

options.text: Endocarditis
options.rationale: Endocarditis can cause MR via leaflet destruction but is not the lecture's most common cause; it would be correct only with documented infection.

options.text: Papillary muscle rupture
options.rationale: Papillary muscle rupture causes acute MR but is not the most common chronic cause; it would be correct only in acute ischemic settings.

options.text: Annular calcification from aging
options.rationale: Annular calcification may contribute to MR but is not the most common cause per the lecture; it would be correct only with imaging confirming annular disease.

question: A 72-year-old patient with severe aortic stenosis is noted to have syncope on exertion, angina, and progressive dyspnea. The lecture gives a prognostic rule related to symptom onset. Which statement best summarizes the prognosis once symptoms develop?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the symptoms and signs of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Once symptomatic, prognosis is poor without surgical correction
options.rationale: The lecture emphasizes that aortic stenosis may be asymptomatic for years but once symptoms like angina, syncope, or CHF appear, prognosis is poor unless surgically corrected.

options.text: Symptoms predict spontaneous improvement without intervention
options.rationale: Spontaneous improvement is unlikely; symptomatic AS typically worsens and requires intervention, so this would be correct only in exceptional cases.

options.text: Symptom onset indicates immediate resolution with medical therapy alone
options.rationale: Medical therapy cannot reverse severe AS; surgery is usually required, so this would be correct only if the lesion were actually regurgitant and responsive to meds.

options.text: Symptoms are unrelated to valve severity and do not affect prognosis
options.rationale: Symptoms correlate with severity and prognosis in AS; this would be correct only if symptoms were due to noncardiac causes.

options.text: Symptom onset mandates only watchful waiting
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is inappropriate once significant symptoms develop in AS; this would be correct only if surgery were absolutely contraindicated.

question: A 59-year-old patient with chronic mitral regurgitation develops atrial fibrillation. According to the lecture, which management step is specifically recommended in this scenario?
cited_learning_objective: Outline a treatment plan for mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Initiate anticoagulation for stroke prevention
options.rationale: The lecture advises anticoagulation when atrial fibrillation occurs in mitral stenosis or regurgitation to reduce thromboembolic risk.

options.text: Immediate mitral valve replacement without anticoagulation
options.rationale: Immediate surgery is not mandated solely by AF; anticoagulation is indicated and surgery is considered based on LV size/function and MR severity.

options.text: Stop all antihypertensive medications
options.rationale: Stopping antihypertensives is not recommended and could worsen hemodynamics; it would be correct only with specific contraindications.

options.text: Begin high‑dose corticosteroids for valve inflammation
options.rationale: Steroids are not standard therapy for chronic MR with AF unless an inflammatory cause like active rheumatic disease were present; it would be correct only with active inflammatory etiology.

options.text: Start lifelong dual antiplatelet therapy instead of anticoagulation
options.rationale: Antiplatelet therapy alone is inadequate for AF stroke prevention in valvular disease; anticoagulation is preferred and this would be correct only if anticoagulation were contraindicated.

question: A 48-year-old man with pulmonary hypertension develops a high‑pitched blowing diastolic murmur best heard at the left second intercostal space. The lecture names an eponymous murmur associated with pulmonic regurgitation. Which murmur is this?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the symptoms and signs of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Graham Steell murmur
options.rationale: The lecture identifies the Graham Steell murmur as a high‑pitched, blowing diastolic murmur heard best at the second left intercostal space in pulmonic regurgitation secondary to pulmonary hypertension.

options.text: Austin Flint murmur
options.rationale: Austin Flint murmur is associated with aortic regurgitation and an apical low‑pitched diastolic sound, not pulmonic regurgitation; it would be correct only with AR findings.

options.text: Duroziez murmur
options.rationale: Duroziez sign is a femoral to‑and‑fro murmur in aortic regurgitation, not the pulmonic diastolic murmur; it would be correct only with femoral findings.

options.text: Corrigan pulse
options.rationale: Corrigan pulse is a peripheral bounding pulse in AR, not a pulmonic diastolic murmur; it would be correct only with AR peripheral signs.

options.text: Opening snap
options.rationale: An opening snap is seen in mitral stenosis, not pulmonic regurgitation; it would be correct only with MS features.

question: A 63-year-old man with severe aortic stenosis is being evaluated for symptom provocation during maneuvers. According to the lecture, how does squatting typically affect the intensity of the systolic murmur of aortic outflow obstruction?
cited_learning_objective: Review of Basic Concepts

options.text: Squatting increases venous return and typically intensifies the murmur
options.rationale: Squatting increases preload and afterload, augmenting flow across the stenotic valve and usually increasing the intensity of the aortic stenosis murmur, consistent with hemodynamic principles reviewed in the lecture.

options.text: Squatting decreases murmur intensity by reducing preload
options.rationale: Squatting actually increases preload rather than reducing it; this option would be correct only if the maneuver decreased venous return.

options.text: Squatting has no effect on murmur intensity in outflow obstruction
options.rationale: Squatting alters hemodynamics and typically changes murmur intensity; it would be correct only if the lesion were completely flow‑independent.

options.text: Squatting converts the murmur to a diastolic sound
options.rationale: Squatting does not change a systolic crescendo–decrescendo murmur into a diastolic murmur; this would be correct only with a different valvular lesion.

options.text: Squatting causes immediate disappearance of the murmur
options.rationale: The murmur does not typically disappear with squatting; disappearance would be correct only if flow across the valve ceased.

question: A 54-year-old woman with chronic aortic regurgitation is noted to have uvular pulsation synchronous with systole. Which eponymous sign from the lecture corresponds to this finding?
cited_learning_objective: Identify the symptoms and signs of mitral, aortic, tricuspid and pulmonic valve disease.

options.text: Muller sign
options.rationale: Muller sign is pulsation of the uvula during systole and is listed among peripheral signs of aortic regurgitation in the lecture.

options.text: Musset sign
options.rationale: Musset sign is head bobbing with each pulse, not uvular pulsation; it would be correct only if head bobbing were observed.

options.text: Quincke pulse
options.rationale: Quincke pulse refers to nailbed capillary pulsations, not uvular movement; it would be correct only with nailbed findings.

options.text: Duroziez sign
options.rationale: Duroziez sign is a femoral to‑and‑fro murmur, not uvular pulsation; it would be correct only with femoral auscultation findings.

options.text: Corrigan pulse
options.rationale: Corrigan pulse is a bounding peripheral pulse with rapid upstroke and collapse, not uvular pulsation; it would be correct only with carotid pulse findings.
